food.text: The sweet potato is a South American plant, yet Polynesians were growing it before Europeans arrived. Current thinking is that it reached central Polynesia around 700 AD, possibly carried by Polynesians who had traveled to South America and back.
Sweet potato was brought to central Polynesia around 700 AD, even though the crop originally came from South America. From there it spread further across Polynesia, reaching Hawaii and New Zealand.

Across Polynesia, Micronesia, and Melanesia, people made a ceremonial drink called kava by grinding the plant's root and mixing it with water or coconut milk, then straining it into a communal bowl to share. The drink numbed the mouth and produced relaxing effects without the cognitive impairment linked to alcohol.
Taro, the staple starch of traditional Polynesian cuisine, was prepared in many ways. Cooks baked it, boiled it, fried it, or steamed it in earth ovens known as umu or imu.

Breadfruit spread into Oceania through the Austronesian expansion and was selectively bred in Polynesia from the breadnut. This produced mostly seedless varieties that became a staple food across the Pacific islands.

In the Cook Islands, sweet potatoes have been radiocarbon-dated to 1000 CE. Some researchers cite this as evidence that Native Americans could have traveled to Oceania, though others argue the plant could have crossed the Pacific by natural dispersal alone.

Taro leaves were commonly cooked wrapped around ingredients such as onion and coconut milk. Both raw and cooked taro roots were also ceremonially presented at chiefly rites and communal events such as weddings and funerals.

Polynesian double-hulled canoes had space between their two hulls to store food, hunting materials, and nets. This let voyagers carry provisions on long ocean crossings, such as those that settled the Cook Islands before 1000 AD.
Sweet potato has been radiocarbon-dated in the Cook Islands to 1000 AD. It is thought to have spread from central Polynesia across the region to Hawaii and New Zealand.

Many researchers believe Polynesian settlers reached Easter Island around the year 800. As they cleared land to plant crops, the rats they had brought with them multiplied, and together with the clearing this gradually caused the island's deforestation.
The very name kava comes from Tongan and Marquesan words meaning 'bitter'. The name reflects the sharp taste and numbing bite of the ceremonial drink made from the plant's root.

art.text: Polynesian voyagers carried the paper mulberry tree from Southeast Asia to make tapa, a beaten barkcloth. By about 1000 AD, tapa cloth was already being made across Western Polynesia, in Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, before it spread to islands farther across the Pacific.

The Saudeleur dynasty united an estimated 25,000 people on the Pacific island of Pohnpei. It ruled from about AD 500 from its ceremonial seat at Nan Madol, a site of small artificial islands linked by canals often called the 'Venice of the Pacific.'

Nan Madol, the canal-linked artificial islands that served as the Saudeleur dynasty's capital, had first seen human activity as early as the first or second century AD. Construction of its islets did not begin until centuries later, by the 8th or 9th century.

Nan Madol's original name was Soun Nan-leng, meaning 'Reef of Heaven,' according to one account. Its network of stone and coral islets bordered by tidal canals later earned it nicknames such as the 'Eighth Wonder of the World' and the 'Venice of the Pacific.'

war.text: On Tongatapu, as the population grew to between 17,000 and 25,000 people, chiefdoms arose to protect against increasing competition for resources. Little else is known about this period, since detailed archaeological evidence is scarce.
In 950 AD, the first Tu'i Tonga, 'Aho'eitu, began expanding his rule beyond Tonga's own shores. Oral tradition suggests Tongatapu's consolidation under his line may date to around the same year.

literature.text: Around 950 CE, the first Tuʻi Tonga, ʻAhoʻeitu, began expanding his rule beyond Tonga. Tongan and Samoan oral tradition, as noted by scholar Dr. ʻOkusitino Mahina, held that ʻAhoʻeitu was the son of the god Tangaloa.

In the 'orthodox' version of the Māori oral tradition, Kupe was a great chief of Hawaiki who arrived in New Zealand in 925 CE. He left his cousin Hoturapa to drown during a fishing expedition and kidnapped his wife, Kūrāmarotini, fleeing with her in her great canoe Matahourua. On their journeys they overcame numerous monsters and sea demons, including the great octopus Te Wheke-a-Muturangi.

The Hawaiian kapu system is thought to have originated among Tahitians and other Pacific Islanders who settled Hawaiʻi sometime between 500 and 1300 AD. One Hawaiian creation myth, the Kumulipo, is an epic chant linking Hawaiian royalty, or aliʻi, to the gods.

Tongan oral tradition placed the origin of the divine father ʻAhoʻeitu around 900 AD, saying he first resided at Popua in the Hahake district. He was said to have later lived in other places nearby, such as Toloa near Fuaʻamotu.
After his voyage, oral tradition says Kupe returned to Hawaiki and told of his adventures discovering New Zealand. His stories persuaded others to migrate with him to the newfound land.

The Kumulipo divided its account of creation into two sections, pō, or night, representing divinity, and ao, or day, representing humankind. This structure reflected mankind's shift from being mere symbols of the gods into the keepers of those symbols, such as idols.

A tradition recorded by Te Hukahuka on 25 October 1847 says that when Kupe first reached the island he found no people there, only 'a flock of spirits' and two birds, a fantail and a kōkako. He then returned to Hawaiki after telling this to a man named Turi.

The Kumulipo, Hawaiʻi's epic creation chant, was recited during the Makahiki season to honor Lono, the god of fertility. This oral tradition linked the sacred chant directly to seasonal ritual practice.

In the Kumulipo's genealogy, after the birth of Laʻilaʻi, the first woman, and Kiʻi, the first man, Kiʻi succeeded in seducing and reproducing with Laʻilaʻi before the god Kāne had a chance. This made the divine lineage of the gods younger than, and therefore subservient to, the lineage of humankind.

science.text: Almost every plant and animal the Austronesians carried across the Pacific came from Southeast Asia, but the sweet potato came from South or Central America. Charred tubers from a 10th-century habitat on Mangaia in the Cook Islands suggest Polynesian navigators reached South America before the year 1000 and brought it back.
Around 700 AD, Austronesian expansion into Polynesia surged again after a long pause. Settlers reached the Cook Islands, Tahiti and the Marquesas by 700 AD, Hawaii by 900 AD, and Rapa Nui by 1000 AD.

Linguistic, biological and archaeological evidence supports a long Polynesian migration from Southeast Asia through the Fijian, Samoan and Tongan archipelagos. The voyagers used outrigger canoes up to twenty or thirty metres long, which could carry families as well as domestic animals.

For a few centuries, the Polynesian islands were connected by bidirectional long-distance sailing. The exception was Rapa Nui, which had limited further contact because of its isolated geographical location.

politics.text: In the 9th century, the Tui Manuʻa controlled a vast maritime empire that took in most of the settled islands of Polynesia. Samoan and Manuʻa oral literature describes a widespread Polynesian network, or confederacy, ruled by successive Tui Manuʻa dynasties.

As Samoa's Tui Manuʻa maritime empire began to decline, a new power rose from the south. In about 950 AD, the first Tuʻi Tonga, ʻAhoʻeitu, began to expand his rule beyond Tonga, starting what is now called the Tuʻi Tonga Empire.

Starting around AD 500, the Saudeleur dynasty united Pohnpei's estimated 25,000 people under one rule. Their capital, Nan Madol, was a lagoon city of small artificial islands linked by canals, later nicknamed the Venice of the Pacific.

From 950 AD, the Tu'i Tonga ruler 'Aho'eitu began extending Tongan rule beyond Tonga. As his influence spread throughout the Pacific, neighboring islands took part in widespread trade of resources and new ideas with Tonga.

The Tuʻi Tonga Empire was centred on the island of Tongatapu, with its capital at Muʻa. Its expansionism and projected hegemony in Oceania began around 950 CE, and researchers point to transoceanic trade and cultural exchange as evidence of its widespread influence.

According to scholar Dr. ʻOkusitino Mahina, Tongan and Samoan oral traditions indicate that the first Tuʻi Tonga was the son of their god Tangaloa. This gave the new dynasty a divine origin shared by both Tonga and Samoa.
Oral tradition holds that Tongatapu was eventually consolidated under a single ruler. He was the first of the Tu'i Tonga line, whose 39-generation lineage may stretch back as far as 950 AD.

Historians speculate that the Tui Manuʻa dynasty grew through its success in controlling oceanic trade in currency goods. These included finely woven ceremonial mats, whale ivory tabua, obsidian and basalt tools, chiefly red feathers, and seashells reserved for royalty, such as polished nautilus and the egg cowry.

The Tui Manuʻa is one of the oldest Samoan titles. Manuan genealogies and religious oral literature suggest its holders had long been among the most prestigious and powerful paramount rulers of Samoa.

The Manuʻa islands of Samoa were the ancestral homeland of the Tuʻi Tonga dynasty and the abode of deities such as Tagaloa ʻEitumatupuʻa. Because of this, the early Tongan kings considered them sacred.

philosophy.text: Native Hawaiian religion, known as the kapu system, was based partly on the tapu system common across Polynesia. It likely originated among Tahitians and other Pacific Islanders who landed in Hawaii sometime between 500 and 1300 CE.

Early Hawaiian religion resembled other Polynesian religions in focusing on natural forces like the tides, the sky, and volcanic activity. Its major gods reflected this: Kāne ruled the sky and creation, Kū war and male pursuits, Lono peace, rain, and fertility, and Kanaloa the ocean.

Marae Taputapuatea, a large complex at Opoa on the eastern coast of Raiatea, may have been established as early as AD 1000. It was once considered the central temple and religious center of Eastern Polynesia.

Evidence suggests Hawaii's earliest Polynesian settlers arrived no later than 800 CE, coming from the Marquesas and greater Polynesia. These settlers carried the roots of what would become the Hawaiian religion.

At Taputapuatea, priests and navigators from all over the Pacific gathered to offer sacrifices to the gods, and to share their knowledge of the genealogical origins of the universe and of deep-ocean navigation. The sacrifices included human sacrifices to 'Oro, the god of life and death, and the drum Ta'imoana was used during them.

Later, within the broader migration window of 500 to 1300 CE, a significant influx of Tahitian settlers landed in Hawaii, bringing their own religious beliefs. Their traditions blended into what became the Hawaiian religion.

culture.text: The Pacific Islands were among the last regions of the world to be permanently settled by humans, reached during the 1st millennium AD. Around 700 CE another surge of island colonization began, carrying Polynesian voyagers far beyond Fiji, Samoa and Tonga.

Polynesian culture is usually divided into four historical eras. After exploration and settlement from about 1800 BC to about AD 700 came a long era of development in isolation, lasting from about 700 to 1595, before Europeans arrived.
Polynesian settlers spread quickly after 700 CE. They reached the Cook Islands, Tahiti and the Marquesas by 700 CE, Hawaii by 900 CE, and Rapa Nui by 1000 CE.

For a few centuries, the Polynesian islands were linked by long-distance sailing that went in both directions. The exception was Rapa Nui, whose isolated location left it with limited further contact.
